answers.primary: A remote MCP server for the error-tracking vendor, added as an HTTP transport (`claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>`) and authenticated per engineer through the server's OAuth 2.0 flow, exactly the shape the docs use for the Sentry example. Each person signs in from `/mcp` inside a session or with `claude mcp login <name>`, and Claude Code stores and refreshes the resulting token itself; no shared key is configured. Scope it `user` if every project should see it, or `project` via `.mcp.json` if only some repos should.
answers.rejected_alternative: Adding the same HTTP server with a static `--header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"`, which is the long-lived-API-key shape the team explicitly wants to avoid, and which also suppresses OAuth: if the server rejects a configured `headers.Authorization`, Claude Code reports the connection as failed rather than falling back to the browser flow.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code owns connecting the server, running the browser OAuth flow, storing the credential outside the config, refreshing it on a 401 and retrying once, and marking the server as needing authentication in `/mcp`. The model only chooses to call the resulting tools.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context. With tool search on by default, only the server's tool names and its server-instructions string load at session start; full schemas and tool results cross into the conversation on demand. Credentials never cross into context: they live in the OS keychain or the credentials file, and MCP results are capped (warning above 10,000 tokens, 25,000-token default limit via `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`).
answers.lifecycle: Claude Code connects the server at every session start for the scope it was added in, and reconnects with exponential backoff if an HTTP server drops mid-session. It stops applying when the engineer runs `claude mcp logout` or clears authentication in `/mcp`, when the server is toggled off, or when it is removed with `claude mcp remove`.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the specific capability and stays visible: an unauthenticated server shows `! Needs authentication` in `claude mcp list` and a startup notice, and its tools are simply unavailable rather than silently wrong. The sharp edge is non-interactive use, where there is no `/mcp` panel and Claude Code cannot run the OAuth flow at all; it can only tell Claude the tools are unavailable until someone authorizes from an interactive session. A rejected refresh token also drops the server mid-session until the engineer re-authenticates.
answers.version_caveat: `claude mcp login`/`logout` from the shell requires v2.1.186 or later, and its no-browser URL-paste path v2.1.191. The startup notice for servers needing sign-in requires v2.1.193. Transient-refresh-failure recovery landed in v2.1.206, and the re-authenticate prompt on a rejected refresh token in v2.1.195. The non-interactive message telling Claude which server needs sign-in requires v2.1.196. Use HTTP, not the deprecated SSE transport, since OAuth is documented for HTTP servers.

answers.primary: LSP, delivered as a code-intelligence plugin: install the official `typescript-lsp` plugin (or ship an in-house plugin whose `.lsp.json` maps `.ts`/`.tsx` to `typescript-language-server`). This is the mechanism whose stated purpose is instant diagnostics pushed into Claude's context after each edit plus go-to-definition, find-references, and hover, replacing symbol-name grepping.
answers.rejected_alternative: A `PostToolUse` hook on `Write|Edit` that shells out to `tsc --noEmit` and returns errors. It can surface type errors after an edit, but it is a full-project recompile per edit with no navigation capability at all, so it does not address the jump-to-definition half of the requirement.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code starts and supervises the language-server process, injects diagnostics into context after edits (the `diagnostics` field defaults to true), and answers navigation requests through the LSP tool. The model does not decide whether diagnostics appear.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context, and cheaply: diagnostics arrive after file edits, symbol locations arrive on lookup, and the docs note symbol lookups often replace broad file reads so net context use can fall. The language server itself runs as a separate subprocess over stdio, so only the diagnostic text and lookup results cross the boundary. Subagents get their own context and do not inherit the main session's diagnostic stream.
answers.lifecycle: The server starts when the session starts with the plugin enabled, restarts on crash by default (bounded by `maxRestarts`), and stops at session end or when the plugin is disabled. Diagnostics apply per edit for the whole session; setting `diagnostics: false` keeps navigation but stops the automatic injection.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, which is the real risk here: if `typescript-language-server` is not installed on the engineer's machine the server never starts, the `/plugin` Errors tab shows `Executable not found in $PATH`, and Claude quietly reverts to grepping with no type feedback at all. A second silent failure is extension collision, where two enabled plugins both claim `.ts` and only the first registered one runs. Diagnostics also inform rather than block: nothing stops Claude from committing code the language server flagged.
answers.version_caveat: The language-server binary must be installed separately (`npm install -g typescript-language-server typescript`); the plugin only wires up the connection. `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require v2.1.205 or later, and before v2.1.205 setting either one made Claude Code skip the LSP server entirely with the reason visible only under `claude --debug`. Also before v2.1.205, a server that failed to initialize still claimed its extensions and blocked a valid competitor.

answers.primary: A plugin, distributed through a team plugin marketplace. One plugin bundles all four pieces in their native component slots: agents/skills for the code-review helpers, `skills/` or `commands/` for the reusable workflow commands, `hooks/hooks.json` for the edit-time automations, and a plugin-root `.mcp.json` for the shared external-tool configuration. Each repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` carries `extraKnownMarketplaces` pointing at the marketplace git source plus `enabledPlugins` naming `<plugin>@<marketplace>`, so cloning any repo surfaces the offer.
answers.rejected_alternative: Copying loose `.claude/` content (skills, `settings.json` hooks, `.mcp.json`) into every repository. It works per repo but has no update channel: the docs' own comparison notes standalone `.claude/` content is available in one project only and must be manually copied to share, which is exactly the maintenance burden the platform team is trying to avoid.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code reads `extraKnownMarketplaces` and `enabledPlugins` from repository settings, prompts on folder trust, clones and caches the marketplace, and loads the plugin's components. The model consumes the components but does not decide whether they are present.
answers.context_boundary: Mixed, by component. Skill and agent descriptions load into the main session at startup with full bodies pulled on use; MCP tool names load at startup with schemas deferred behind tool search; hooks run entirely out of context in their own subprocesses and cross the boundary only through whatever they print back. Agents run in their own isolated context and return summaries.
answers.lifecycle: The marketplace-install prompt fires when the engineer trusts the folder, then a second prompt offers the plugins; the choices are recorded in user settings so skipped marketplaces and plugins stay skipped. Components apply for every session in which the plugin is enabled, and stop when it is disabled in `enabledPlugins` at any scope (or `.claude/settings.local.json` for a per-machine opt-out). Updates arrive via `/plugin update` or background auto-update.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open per engineer, which is the gap against "everyone gets the same set". Enabling a plugin from an external source in a project's `.claude/settings.json` does not install it for other people: as of v2.1.195 every load path asks each user to install and trust the plugin first, so anyone who declines or skips silently runs without the review helpers and hooks and nothing reports the divergence. Project settings also outrank user settings, so a personal `false` will not opt someone out of a project-enabled plugin unless they use local settings.
answers.version_caveat: The per-user install-and-trust gate on every plugin load path requires v2.1.195; earlier versions behaved differently. `displayName` requires v2.1.143 and `defaultEnabled` v2.1.154. If the platform team needs the set to be mandatory rather than offered, that is managed settings territory (`enabledPlugins` force-enabled in managed settings, which also exempts the plugin's hooks from `allowManagedHooksOnly`), not repository settings.

answers.primary: A plugin, using its `bin/` directory. Executables placed in `bin/` at the plugin root are added to the Bash tool's `PATH` while the plugin is enabled, so the deployment CLI is invokable as a bare command in any Bash tool call and composes normally with `grep` and `jq` in a pipeline. Ship the binary in the existing shared toolkit plugin and install that plugin at user scope so it applies across every project.
answers.rejected_alternative: Wrapping the CLI in a bundled MCP server that exposes each subcommand as a tool. That gives Claude typed access but destroys the actual requirement: MCP tool results come back as tool output, not as a process in a shell pipeline, so the binary can never be composed with `grep` and `jq` in a single Bash invocation.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code is what prepends the plugin's `bin/` to the Bash tool's `PATH` for the lifetime of the plugin being enabled. The model just writes an ordinary command line and does not need to know where the binary lives.
answers.context_boundary: Essentially nothing extra crosses the boundary. The binary lives on disk in the plugin cache and executes in the Bash tool's subprocess; only the command's stdout/stderr enters the conversation, the same as any other shell command. There is no schema, no description, and no per-session token cost, which is the main advantage over the MCP framing.
answers.lifecycle: The `PATH` entry exists for every Bash tool call in any session where the plugin is enabled, and disappears when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled. It is not tied to a project, a prompt, or a skill invocation. On a plugin update the executable moves to a new `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`; the previous version directory lingers about 14 days before cleanup.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently. The `PATH` injection covers only the Bash tool, not the engineer's own interactive shell, so a person reproducing Claude's command by hand gets `command not found` and concludes the toolkit is broken. Because it is a compiled binary, the plugin has to carry a build matching each user's OS and architecture or the bare command dies at exec time with no configuration error to point at. Permission rules still apply independently: without a `Bash(<tool>:*)` allow rule every invocation prompts.
answers.version_caveat: The mirrored documentation lists `bin/` in the plugin directory structure and file-locations table but states no minimum Claude Code version, no experimental flag, and no plan restriction for it, so I cannot confirm a version gate from the permitted inputs. The one documented scoping limit is that the `PATH` addition applies to the Bash tool only and only while the plugin is enabled.

answers.primary: A plugin distributed from a git-hosted marketplace, versioned by commit SHA: omit the `version` field from both `plugin.json` and the marketplace entry so Claude Code falls back to the plugin source's git commit SHA as the cache key, and set `"autoUpdate": true` on the marketplace entry in `extraKnownMarketplaces` so Claude Code refreshes the marketplace and updates installed plugins in the background after startup. This is precisely the documented approach for internal or team plugins under active development.
answers.rejected_alternative: An explicit semantic `version` in `plugin.json`. It is the right choice for a published plugin with a stable release cycle, but here it inverts the requirement: pushing new commits without bumping the field has no effect and `/plugin update` reports "already at the latest version", so every daily change would need a manual bump, which is exactly the release bookkeeping the team wants to eliminate.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code computes the current version, compares it against the cached copy, clones or refreshes the marketplace repository, and swaps in the new plugin cache directory. The model has no role in the update path at all.
answers.context_boundary: Outside the conversation entirely. The refresh runs in the background after startup, against the marketplace git source and the plugin cache under `~/.claude/plugins/cache`. What crosses into context is only the effect: the newer skills, agents, and tool definitions the next session loads.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by background auto-update after session startup, or on demand by `/plugin update`. A mid-session update does not take effect immediately: hook commands, monitors, MCP servers, and LSP servers keep using the previous version's path until `/reload-plugins`, and monitors need a full session restart. Superseded version directories are marked orphaned and removed 14 days later so already-running sessions keep working.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, with no gate between a merge and every teammate's machine. Any commit that lands, including a broken hook or a bad manifest, propagates to everyone on their next startup with no review, no pin, and no staged rollout, and the teammate finds out when a component stops loading. Commit-SHA versioning also only works for git-backed sources (`github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, relative paths in a git-hosted marketplace); an `npm` source or a local directory outside a git repo resolves to `unknown` and the update check has nothing to compare.
answers.version_caveat: `autoUpdate` must be set explicitly: when omitted it defaults to `true` only for official Anthropic marketplaces and `false` for every other marketplace, so an internal marketplace that does not set it will never refresh in the background. `skipLfs` on the marketplace source requires v2.1.153. The 14-day orphan retention is what makes concurrent sessions survive an update, so do not treat the old cache directory as durable state.

answers.primary: An MCP server entry of type `http` pointing at the internal service, with `headersHelper` set to the SSO helper command. Claude Code runs the command at connection time and merges the JSON object it prints on stdout into the connection headers, which is the documented path for authentication schemes that are not OAuth, specifically naming short-lived tokens and internal SSO.
answers.rejected_alternative: A static `headers` block with environment-variable expansion, such as `"Authorization": "Bearer ${SSO_TOKEN}"` in `.mcp.json`. Expansion happens once when the configuration is read, so the token is frozen at whatever value the environment held at startup and the connection breaks the moment it expires mid-session, which is the exact failure the team described.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper, applies its output as headers, and (from v2.1.193) re-runs it, reconnects, and retries once when a tool call returns 401 or 403. The model never sees or handles the token.
answers.context_boundary: The token stays outside the model's context entirely. The helper runs as a shell subprocess with a 10-second timeout, from the session's current working directory, with `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME` and `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL` in its environment; only tool results cross into the conversation. If the server is plugin-provided, the helper also gets `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` and runs with its working directory set to the plugin root.
answers.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh on each connection, meaning at session start and on every reconnect, plus on the automatic retry after a 401 or 403. There is no caching, so the script itself owns any token reuse. It stops applying when the server is removed, toggled off, or the plugin providing it is disabled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed at the tool-call boundary but with a narrow recovery window: mid-session expiry is repaired only by the single 401/403 retry, and if that retry also fails the server is flagged as needing authentication in `/mcp` for the rest of the session and its tools go dark. Other real breakages are a helper that exceeds the 10-second timeout, one that prints anything other than a flat JSON object of string key-value pairs, and a relative script path that does not resolve from the session's working directory. Note also that `headersHelper` executes arbitrary shell, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.
answers.version_caveat: Automatic helper re-run plus reconnect and single retry on 401/403 requires v2.1.193 or later; before that an expired token simply broke the connection. For a plugin-provided helper, working-directory resolution at the plugin root and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` substitution into `headersHelper` require v2.1.195. As of v2.1.207 a plugin `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values because the command is shell-parsed; the server is reported as misconfigured instead, so have the script read the value from its own config file or environment.

answers.primary: A plugin background monitor: a `monitors/monitors.json` entry in the shared toolkit plugin with `"command": "tail -F ./logs/error.log"`, a `description`, and the default `"when": "always"`. Claude Code starts the process automatically when the plugin is active and delivers every stdout line to Claude as a notification, which is exactly the "nobody has to ask it to start watching" requirement.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that instructs Claude to invoke the Monitor tool on the log file. It uses the same underlying mechanism, but it is model-initiated: it only runs if Claude decides to invoke it, so the watch is not guaranteed to exist for the whole session and does not start unprompted.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code spawns the monitor process for the session and pushes each stdout line in as a notification. The model owns only what it does with the lines, not whether the watch exists.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context, and this is the cost centre. Every stdout line becomes a notification in the conversation, so the log volume is charged directly against the main context window, and each re-billed turn carries it. The process itself runs in the session working directory, unsandboxed, at the same trust level as hooks; it appears in the task panel with its `description`.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at session start and again on plugin reload; runs as a persistent background process for the lifetime of the session. The `name` field prevents duplicate processes on reload. Disabling the plugin mid-session does not stop an already-running monitor: it stops only when the session ends. After a plugin update the monitor keeps using the old plugin path until a full session restart, since `/reload-plugins` does not switch monitors.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and unbounded. There is no rate limit or filter described, so a noisy error log floods the context window and can crowd out the actual work, and a monitor that dies just stops delivering with no enforcement that Claude notices. It is also silently absent in several environments: monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions, are skipped where the Monitor tool is unavailable, and do not load at all for a project-scope skills-directory plugin. Because it runs unsandboxed, a bad command is a real execution risk, not just a missing feature.
answers.version_caveat: Monitors are an experimental plugin component; declare them under `experimental.monitors` in `plugin.json` (the top-level key still works but `claude plugin validate` warns and a future release will require the `experimental.*` form), and the manifest schema may change between releases. As of v2.1.207 a monitor command cannot reference `${user_config.*}` and monitor processes do not receive `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>` variables, so the script must read configurable values from a file it owns.

answers.primary: The MCP server's `oauth.scopes` field, pinned to the read-only subset in the server's configuration entry, for example `"oauth": { "scopes": "issues:read search:read" }`. This is the documented supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant, and it constrains the token that is actually minted and stored rather than constraining behaviour after the fact.
answers.rejected_alternative: Permission `deny` rules on the write-shaped tool names from that server. That only stops Claude Code from issuing the call; the credential on disk would still carry write and admin authority, so anything else that reads it, or any path around the rule, could write. The requirement was explicitly stronger than "the assistant declines".
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, and worth stating plainly: Claude Code (the harness) owns requesting the pinned scope set during the authorization flow, but the actual guarantee is owned by the vendor's authorization server, which must honour the down-scoped `scope` parameter and issue a correspondingly limited token. The model owns nothing here.
answers.context_boundary: No conversation context is involved. The pinning lives in the server's configuration entry (`.mcp.json`, `~/.claude.json`, or the plugin's MCP config) and takes effect in the browser authorization flow; the resulting token is stored in the keychain or credentials file and never enters the model's context. Only the tools the granted scopes permit surface in the session.
answers.lifecycle: Applies at authorization time, so it binds when the engineer first signs in and on every re-authentication. If the server returns a 403 `insufficient_scope` for a tool call, Claude Code re-authenticates with the same pinned scopes rather than widening them, so the restriction survives the retry path. It stops applying if someone edits or removes `oauth.scopes` and re-authenticates, or clears authentication and signs in fresh against an unpinned config.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for capability (a tool needing an unpinned scope keeps 403-ing and the loop re-authenticates with the same narrow set until someone widens the config), but the security guarantee itself can fail open in one specific way: pinning is a client-side request, so if the identity provider ignores the `scope` parameter or issues a broader token anyway, the stored credential is wider than intended and nothing local detects it. Verify the issued token's actual grants with the vendor. Two more sharp edges: `offline_access` is appended automatically when the authorization server advertises it, and the config file is editable by the engineer, so this is a policy control, not a tamper-proof one, unless it is deployed through managed settings.
answers.version_caveat: `oauth.scopes` takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and anything discovered at `/.well-known`. As of v2.1.196, with `oauth.scopes` unset, Claude Code requests only the scope from the `WWW-Authenticate` header or protected resource metadata and no longer asks for the full `scopes_supported` catalog; before that it requested the catalog, which is exactly how admin-only scopes ended up in the request. Scopes fetched from a configured `authServerMetadataUrl` still supply `scopes_supported` as the requested set, so do not combine the two casually. These OAuth fields apply to HTTP and SSE transports only.

answers.primary: A project-scoped MCP server: a `.mcp.json` file at the repository root defining the staging-database server, checked into version control, added with `claude mcp add --scope project`. Project scope loads only in that project and is shared with the team through the repository, which matches both halves of the requirement (fresh clone picks it up, no other repository ever sees it).
answers.rejected_alternative: User scope (`claude mcp add --scope user`, stored in `~/.claude.json`). It is private to each engineer and reaches nothing from a clone, and it loads the staging-database connection in every project on the machine, which the requirement rules out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code reads `.mcp.json`, holds the server at pending approval until the person accepts it, records that choice, and connects the server. The model neither sees the pending server's tools nor can bypass the approval.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context of any session started in that repository. Only tool names and server instructions load at startup with tool search on; schemas and results cross on demand. Credentials referenced through `${VAR}` expansion in `env`, `url`, or `headers` come from the engineer's own environment rather than from the checked-in file, so secrets stay out of the repository.
answers.lifecycle: Approval is requested the first time the server is used and the decision persists per project, so each person consents exactly once; `claude mcp reset-project-choices` clears those decisions. The server connects at every session start in that project thereafter, and stops applying if the person toggles it off, adds it to `disabledMcpjsonServers`, or the entry is removed from `.mcp.json`.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, and the first-clone experience is the practical friction: a freshly cloned repository cannot approve its own servers. As of v2.1.196, `enableAllProjectMcpServers` or `enabledMcpjsonServers` committed to the project's `.claude/settings.json` is ignored in an untrusted folder, so the server sits at `⏸ Pending approval (run \`claude\` to approve)` in `claude mcp list` until the engineer runs `claude` interactively and accepts the workspace trust dialog. A `disabledMcpjsonServers` entry in any settings file rejects the server outright. If a referenced environment variable is unset with no `:-default`, the config still loads but Claude Code warns and passes the literal `${VAR}` through, so the server fails to connect for a reason that looks like a credential problem.
answers.version_caveat: The untrusted-folder approval behaviour requires v2.1.196 or later; approvals from user settings, managed settings, and `--settings` still apply in an untrusted folder, and an untracked `.claude/settings.local.json` applies only after a trust dialog as of v2.1.207. If the entry is an HTTP server, give it an explicit `"type": "http"`: a `url` with no `type` is a configuration error that Claude Code skips, and before v2.1.202 it reported that as a confusing `command: expected string, received undefined`.

answers.primary: A `SessionStart` hook in the plugin that installs into the persistent data directory: it diffs the bundled `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json` against a stored copy in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` and, when they differ, copies the manifest and runs `npm install` there. Plugin scripts and MCP servers then point at the persisted tree, for example `"env": { "NODE_PATH": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules" }`. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` resolves to `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/` and survives plugin updates by design.
answers.rejected_alternative: Installing `node_modules` into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` at first run. That path changes on every plugin update, so the modules are stranded with the old version directory, which is marked orphaned and cleaned up about 14 days later. The docs say plainly to treat it as ephemeral and not write state there.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code fires `SessionStart` and runs the hook command as a subprocess with `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` and `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA` exported. The model is not involved in the install and should not be asked to run it.
answers.context_boundary: Outside the conversation. The hook runs in its own process and nothing crosses into context unless the hook deliberately prints text back, which this one should not; keep it quiet so a routine npm install does not consume session context. The installed modules live under the user's `~/.claude/plugins/data/`, not in the repository or the plugin cache.
answers.lifecycle: Fires at every session start, including on `--continue`/`--resume` with `source` set to `resume` (or `fork`). The manifest diff makes it a cheap no-op after the first successful install and a real reinstall only when a plugin update ships a changed `package.json`. The data directory is deleted when the plugin is uninstalled from the last scope where it is installed, unless `--keep-data` is passed; the `/plugin` interface shows its size and prompts before deleting.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly. A failed `npm install` (offline machine, proxy, private registry auth) leaves the modules missing and the failure only surfaces later, when a plugin script or MCP server dies on a missing require. The trailing `rm -f "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json"` in the documented command is load-bearing: it removes the copied manifest so the next session retries instead of believing the install succeeded. A directory-existence check alone is the wrong test, because the data directory outlives every plugin version and so cannot detect a changed dependency manifest.
answers.version_caveat: Do not rely on the `Setup` hook for this: it only fires with `--init-only`, or with `--init`/`--maintenance` in `-p` mode, so it does not run on ordinary launches. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` is created on first reference. When a plugin updates mid-session, hooks and MCP servers keep using the previous version's path until `/reload-plugins`. The mirrored documentation states no minimum Claude Code version for `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` or the persistent data directory, so I cannot confirm a version gate from the permitted inputs.
